## Campeche: Mexico's Fortified City

This fortified city stands on the western coast of the Yucatán Peninsula. In the first quarter of the 17th century, the area was known as the land of Campeche, after the valuable Campeche (sandalwood) tree that grew here. Famous pirates repeatedly raided this wealthy port.

Campeche is a lovely place for a walk along its picturesque 3.5-kilometer waterfront and the cobbled streets of its historic center, lined with shops, restaurants, bars, and cafés.

## Campeche for Ecotourism Enthusiasts

Nature lovers can explore the nearby Ría Celestún reserve, home to hundreds of pink flamingos. Another attraction is Calakmul, one of the country's largest reserves. In addition to hiking and mountain biking, visitors can discover the Maya archaeological site that gave the reserve its name.

Official figures put the drop of Angel Falls at 979 meters, although some researchers argue that the waterfall is even higher, reaching at least 1,054 meters.

It is a breathtaking sight that stays with you long afterward. The view from the air is especially impressive, while adventure seekers may be drawn to the hike up to the falls. Dense tropical forest surrounds the waterfall, punctuated by isolated cliffs. The park's jungle is rich in endemic plants and animals.

The small town of Canaima lies in the heart of the national park, with several smaller but remarkably scenic waterfalls nearby. The 105-meter Salto Aponwao waterfall is also found here. To experience this natural wonder, visitors need to travel by canoe.

## Cancún: One of Mexico's Finest Resorts

This distinctive destination lies on the Caribbean coast. Located on the Yucatán Peninsula, Cancún is ranked among the world's ten best resorts.

Over the past two decades, Cancún has grown from a small village in the jungle into one of the world's best-known international resorts, celebrated for its clean beaches, crystal-clear water, and monuments of Indigenous culture.

## Cancún Offers More Than a Beach Holiday

Just a two-hour drive away is Chichén Itzá, the capital of a vanished Maya empire. Cancún has a highly developed tourism infrastructure: comfortable stays in ultra-modern hotels along miles of sandy beaches, opportunities to enjoy virtually every kind of sport, restaurants serving Mexican, European, and Asian cuisine, numerous evening shows and nightclubs, and large shopping centers.

Caracas is Venezuela's lively and beautiful capital, one of the relatively young and modern capitals on the map of South America.

The old quarter is a center of cultural and historical architecture, with numerous museums and churches.

For anyone who enjoys street markets, the Parque Central district is a paradise. City authorities have set aside this area for street vendors, where shoppers can find both original goods and crude counterfeits. The district also has many museums and theaters, including the Children's Museum and the Teresa Carreño Theater, described as the third largest in South America.

Venezuela's capital offers visitors an abundance of remarkable places: beautiful churches, fascinating museums, lush gardens, and parks. The neo-Gothic Santa Capilla Church stands out sharply among the city's classical churches. Ávila National Park rises above Caracas like an emerald crown. The beautiful Caribbean coast lies a short distance from the city and is a favorite getaway for residents. The suburb of El Hatillo has preserved many examples of colonial architecture. Another city attraction is La Rinconada, described as South America's largest and most modern racecourse.

Kavac is a canyon in the Auyán-tepui area, within the natural landscape of Canaima. Its defining features are the narrow passage between rock walls, flowing water, and stretches of tropical vegetation above the gorge. Inside the canyon, the broad open landscape gives way to an intimate world of stone and water.

Kavac is part of the region's nature excursion routes. Here the focus is on the gorge's terrain and waterfalls, while the journey there gives visitors a sense of the scale of the savanna and table mountains. A visit adds a close-up experience of the rocky surroundings to the panoramic views of the tepuis.
